questions.title: What Is Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) At Its Core?
questions.question_body: I understand that traditional reinforcement learning from human feedback trains an independent reward model followed by policy optimisation with an RL algorithm such as PPO. In contrast the authors claim that DPO optimises a language‑model policy directly using only a binary cross‑entropy loss over human preference pairs. Can someone explain intuitively why this works – why isn’t an explicit reward worth learning needed?

questions.title: "Partition Function" Cancels When Plugging Into Bradley–Terry
questions.question_body: "Eq.(4)" defines r(x,y)=β log[π_r(y|x)/π_ref(y|x)] + β log Z(x). Substituting this into the Bradley–Terry probability p*(y₁≻y₂|x)=σ(r(y₁)−r(y₂)) gives an expression involving Z(x). How does Z(x) disappear mathematically?

questions.title: "β" – What Is Its Role In The Loss And Resulting Policy?
questions.question_body: "β" appears both as an exponent scaling factor in the optimal policy definition π_r(y|x)= Z⁻¹·π_ref(y|x)e^(r/β) and multiplicatively in front of logs in Eq.(6). Intuitively is β describing how tightly the twisted policy πθ is tied to its reference Π_ref? How change β influences exploration versus exploitation during training?

questions.title: "Actor‑Critic” Instability Despite Equivalent Loss
questions.question_body:
"Theorem 4" shows maximizing E[rϕ−β·KL] leads to Equation (6), i.e., the very same objective solved efficiently by DPO without sampling bursts nor baselines.
Why then do standard actor‑critic methods such as PPO tend to be unreliable – suffering mode collapse or vanishing gradients – whereas vanilla gradient descent on Eq.(6) behaves stably?
